newsitem.title: FRANCE: French oil workers strike, pledge more action.
newsitem.headline: French oil workers strike, pledge more action.

text.p: Disgruntled French oil workers staged new strikes on Tuesday and promised further disruption this week -- but oil firms said unions had failed to carry out a threat to shut down the oil industry for a day.
Key workers walked out at about half of France's refineries, causing them to drop output in a coordinated one-day protest against plans to shed roughly 1,500 jobs over the next year.
But oil industry leaders said the strike had a mixed turnout and caused less hardship for oil firms than a strike at Elf last week or a 12-day blockade of depots by truck drivers last month.
"We lost some output but the strike wasn't well supported," a spokeswoman for oil industry association UFIP said.

Oil majors Shell, British Petroleum, Esso and Total all said at least one of their plants was hit. Total, France's second oil company after Elf, said its network of three plants cut output significantly.
But seven of France's 13 oil refineries took no action, oil companies and unions said.
Unions had promised a full one-day strike to widen pressure on bosses to scrap redundancies after a bitter dispute crippled France's biggest oil firm, Elf Aquitaine, last week.
Unions said they would, however, carry on the protests at two Esso refineries and a Mobil plant later this week.
"We demand the total withdrawal of all redundancy plans," an official at the Communist-backed CGT union said.

Both sides agree 1,500 jobs are on the line in plans already announced to cut overcapacity. Oil firms say the problem is too many plants are pumping out petrol which must be sold at knock-down prices against fierce competition from supermarkets.
Unions say oil firms can solve that without cutting jobs.
Their anger was given an unexpected twist during Tuesday's strike when Anglo-Dutch giant Shell said it was looking at ways of cutting excess refining capacity in southeastern France.
Analysts said that was a clear reference to Shell's Berre refinery near Marseille, the only refinery forced to halt virtually all operations in Tuesday's oil strike.
A union official slammed the timing of Shell's announcement as provocative, saying it might harden the strike.
"You don't discuss this kind of thing when the climate is already hot," he told Reuters.
A Shell France spokesman said the timing was an accident.
He said Shell was not considering plans to axe the plant, merely to share out cuts in capacity with other refiners.

Oil firms complain they have it particularly badly in France because the government has encouraged them through taxes to build complexes for making unleaded petrol (gasoline) but now wants them to produce even cleaner diesel instead.
"We invested five billion francs ($1 billion) in unleaded petrol -- now we have to export it," the UFIP official said.
But unions accuse firms of slashing jobs to boost profits.
